lesson.title: iperf: Finding Out What Your Network Can Actually Carry
lesson.summary: iperf is a tool that actively measures achievable bandwidth between two hosts by generating real test traffic, answering the question packet capture cannot: not what happened, but what the link is capable of.
lesson.body:
Throughput is the amount of data a link actually moves per unit time, and it is very often lower than the number printed on the hardware. A link advertised as 1 Gbps rarely delivers a sustained 1 Gbps of application data, because protocol overhead, congestion, latency, and misconfiguration all eat into the theoretical maximum. The only way to know what a link truly delivers is to push real traffic across it and measure the result, and that is what iperf does.

iperf works as a client-server test: you start an iperf3 server on one host with iperf3 -s, then run the client on the other host pointed at it, for example iperf3 -c 10.0.0.5 -t 10, which sends traffic for ten seconds and reports the achieved throughput. This is a fundamentally different activity from packet capture. Wireshark and tcpdump are passive, they observe traffic that is already happening for some other reason. iperf is active, it generates traffic specifically to measure the network's capacity, which makes it the right tool when the question is not what went wrong, but how much can this link actually do.

Consider a concrete scenario: two servers are connected through switches rated at 1 Gbps each, and you expect close to that speed between them. Running iperf3 -c against the server, you instead measure around 300 Mbps. That gap is a starting point for investigation, not a final answer. A duplex mismatch on one of the links (one side set to full duplex, the other negotiating half duplex) is a classic cause of a large, consistent throughput drop like this. High latency between the hosts combined with a small TCP window can also cap throughput well below the link's physical capacity, because TCP can only have a limited amount of unacknowledged data in flight at once, the bandwidth-delay product, unless window scaling is enabled; running the client with multiple parallel streams (iperf3 -c 10.0.0.5 -P 4) helps distinguish this cause, since parallel streams multiply the effective window and should recover much of the missing throughput if that is the actual bottleneck.

iperf also supports UDP mode, which is useful for a different reason: TCP's own congestion control adjusts its sending rate in response to loss, so a TCP-based test partly measures TCP's behavior, not just the raw link. A UDP test with iperf3 -c 10.0.0.5 -u -b 500M sends at a fixed rate and reports packet loss and jitter directly, which is closer to how a real-time application like voice or video would experience the link, and it connects directly forward to later testing tools: once you can induce loss or delay artificially, for example with tc netem, iperf in UDP mode is exactly how you would measure the effect of that induced loss on throughput and jitter, and a packet capture running alongside the test would show you the retransmissions or gaps causing the numbers you see.
